title: Nonrelativistic quantum theory of non-dipole effects in a multielectron atom: radiation transition operator
abstract: In the work of Hopersky A.N. et al., arXiv: 2609.33494v1 [physics. atom-ph] in the Loudon integral representation, the general analytical structure of the complete operator of a multipole radiation transition taking into account non-dipole effects for a multielectron atom is established. In this Letter this structure is converted to the sum only for all multipoles.

title: Two-photon Doppler-free spectroscopy of the $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6s23s\;^1S_0$ Rydberg transition for quantum sensing in ytterbium
abstract: Here we report atomic structure calculations and experimental observations of the two-photon $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6s23s\;^1S_0$ transition in Yb. The unique level structure of Yb places the $6s6p\;^1P_1$ state's energy at $\approx\!49.7\%$ of the ionization energy, which facilitates two-photon Doppler-free excitation of the $6s23s\;^1S_0$ Rydberg state from the $6s^2\;^1S_0$ ground state at a relatively low optical intensity. This $J= 0 \rightarrow J=0$ transition is immune to first-order Zeeman and electric quadrupole shifts, has reduced sensitivity to higher-order Zeeman shifts, and is further predicted to have relatively low sensitivity to density shifts. Using configuration interaction theory, we compute relevant properties of the $6s23s\;^1S_0$ Rydberg state for sensing, including the $C_6$ coefficient, dc polarizability, blackbody radiation (BBR) shift, and BBR depopulation rate. As a first experimental step, we demonstrate two-photon Doppler-free spectroscopy of the $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6s23s\;^1S_0$ transition. From our experimental spectra, we estimate the natural linewidth (lifetime) of the $6s23s\;^1S_0$ state to be 90 kHz (1.8 $\mu$s). We believe this transition, or other $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6sns\;^1S_0$ transitions in Yb with $n\approx23$, may find use in a variety of sensing applications, potentially including a two-photon clock, electrometer, or BBR thermometer.

title: Ultra-stable laser with sub-Hz intrinsic linewidth using a silicon photonic chip
abstract: Here, we demonstrate a novel optical self-injection-locking scheme integrated with a modulation-free laser frequency stabilization technique co-integrated with a compact vacuum-gap micro-Fabry-Perot cavity (uFP), with Q-factor of 3.46E9, to realize an ultra-stable laser with sub-Hz fundamental linewidth using a silicon photonic chip. The demonstrated electro-optic self-injection locking (EOSIL) chip suppresses a commercial DFB diode laser's frequency noise power spectral density by more than 110 dB at 1 Hz offset, approaching the theoretical thermal noise limit of the uFP cavity, and enables a laser fundamental linewidth of 58 mHz with a fractional frequency instability of 8.68E-13 at 1 sec averaging time. The chip is fabricated using the Advanced Micro Foundry standard silicon photonic process and occupies a footprint of 10 mm^2.

title: Trapping of nanofabricated SiO$_2$ high-aspect-ratio discs in an optical lattice
abstract: We describe the nanofabrication and loading of lithographically patterned, high aspect ratio $10$ $\mu$m diameter silicon dioxide discs with thickness of $400$ nm into an optical standing wave trap in vacuum. We obtain motional spectra of the center of mass motion of the discs using a combination of interferometric and imaging methods. The method is capable of high-efficiency loading and optical trapping using small numbers of objects, of the order of a few particles, with customized geometries and sizes compatible with wafer scale nanofabrication methods. Disc-like particles in optical traps have been identified as promising candidates for detectors of high frequency gravitational waves or as sensitive accelerometers.

title: Managing complexity for integrated fusion reactor design using a differentiable graph-based MDAO framework: PROCESS as a case study
abstract: Integrated design of nuclear fusion reactors requires combining an increasingly large number of models from different disciplines self-consistently, with model selection and parametrisation changing between design studies. Manual definition of execution order and solvers for cyclic dependencies is error-prone, inefficient, and inflexible. We propose to use a generic graph-based coordination and execution core that enables automated execution order, cycle detection, and solver architecture specification for any set of models or parametrisation. To this end, a computational dependency graph of purely functional models is extended by a conditional node and nesting edges, treating solvers and optimisers in the same way. A minimal set of graph operations then allows for fine-tuned control on feedback resolution, making both optimiser and solver architectures easily reconfigurable. Existing monolithic multidisciplinary design analysis and optimisation (MDAO) architectures can be recovered by sequentially applying these operations. The cottax package implements this extended dependency graph, graph operations, executability checks, and a JAX-based execution layer. This execution layer eliminates runtime overhead and provides native gradient computation through the whole graph. As a proof of principle, cottax is then applied to the PROCESS systems code. Graph sequencing shows that for PROCESS only three small coupled components need to be solved every optimiser iteration. Monolithic MDAO architectures are then assigned to seven different PROCESS configurations, demonstrating the ease of (re)configuring its architecture. Compared to PROCESS, the sequencing and execution back-end together yield a two to three orders of magnitude reduction in model runtime during optimisation. cottax is currently being considered as the basis for developing an integrated stellarator MDAO framework.

title: Development of a fabrication-to-benchtop process for SiN-based quantum devices
abstract: Silicon nitride has emerged as a key material for the advancement of future quantum communication and computational devices. However, challenges persist in establishing a comprehensive development process, spanning from fabrication to optical characterization, essential for advancing these devices to their next stage of potential. Maintaining control over the entire process, from start to finish, alongside device modeling, enables more efficient and timely iteration and optimization. Here we introduce a fabrication-to-benchtop process. We employ an in-house stoichiometric recipe for device fabrication and conduct comprehensive characterization of optical losses and material properties. Understanding and controlling the refractive index of the device are vital for predicting device geometries and group indices. Implementing the refractive indices of our fabricated devices, we simulate microring resonators and demonstrate their application in generating optical solitons.

title: Programming the Nonlinear Optics of a Nanoporous Photonic Metamaterial by Confined Crystallization
abstract: A membrane traversed by a dense array of nanochannels acts as a photonic metamaterial: with channels far smaller than the wavelength of light, the optical response is set by the architecture rather than by the constituent materials. Here each nanochannel is turned into a nonlinear optical meta-atom by filling anodic aluminum oxide (AAO) with benzil (BZL), a noncentrosymmetric molecular crystal, and the crystallization pathway programs their orientation. In free-standing membranes every channel solidifies independently, the orientations remain uncorrelated, and the effective second-harmonic generation (SHG) response is nearly polarization isotropic; its magnitude follows a core - shell model in which an optically inactive interfacial layer of 2.6 nm reduces the active volume of each meta-atom, reproducing on bare alumina the value previously found on alkyl-grafted silica and indicating a host-insensitive limit. Seeding crystallization from a bulk benzil layer instead aligns the meta-atoms over submillimeter domains and produces a macroscopically anisotropic effective susceptibility. Channel diameters from 32 to 270 nm span the transition out of the subwavelength regime, and the anomalous directional SHG emission reported here is confined to the metamaterial limit. Confined crystallization thus offers a route to nonlinear optical metamaterials whose effective susceptibility tensor is written during processing.

title: Wavelength Diversity Expands the Expressive Power of Optical Computing
abstract: Universal function approximation underpins neural networks' capacity to represent nonlinear relationships, but realizing this capability in optical hardware requires engineering the computational features encoded in light. Here, we show that wavelength diversity enhances optical function-approximation expressivity through wavelength-scaled Fourier features generated by a shared phase encoder, without increasing the number of input-encoded harmonics. Multiple wavelengths contribute to the representation of each output function rather than merely serving as independent computational channels. We establish theoretical scaling laws and approximation-error bounds, revealing that, for nondispersive encoders, the spectral endpoints determine the accessible computational bandwidth, while intermediate illumination wavelengths enrich the available harmonics within that bandwidth. Numerical studies demonstrate improved approximation of real- and complex-valued nonlinear functions, with a representative design achieving more than a 100-fold reduction in mean-squared error relative to tested monochromatic optical processors with the same number of trainable phase features. Experimentally, we validate enhanced approximation accuracy and demonstrate the simultaneous approximation of 4,136 distinct nonlinear functions using a compact, single-layer diffractive processor under five-wavelength illumination. These results establish wavelength diversity as an additional physical resource for scaling the expressive power of optical computing and enhancing the accuracy of parallel nonlinear function approximation.

title: High average flux positron sources driven by a mJ-class laser
abstract: We report on the production and characterisation of MeV-scale positron populations driven by a high-repetition-rate, mJ-class laser system. The positrons are generated via a two-step Bethe--Heitler process driven by laser-wakefield-accelerated electron beams propagating through a mm-scale lead converter. At 10 Hz, approximately 1000 positrons in the 0.8--1.7 MeV energy range were measured over 100 accumulated shots. Stable electron acceleration was demonstrated at 10 Hz, 100 Hz, and 1 kHz using approximately 9 mJ of laser energy in the focal spot, indicating the potential for substantially higher average positron fluxes for laser systems operating at kHz repetition rates and energies of 10s of mJ. Such a positron source allows generating sufficiently high average fluxes of MeV-scale positrons while maintaining low positron yields per pulse and narrow temporal distributions, a regime of particular interest for novel applications in material science and fundamental physics. The measured positron yields and spectra are in good agreement with Monte Carlo simulations, supporting the modelling of the positron-production process and magnetic transport system.

title: A dry cryogenic platform with picometre stability for nanoscale and quantum technologies
abstract: Mechanically ultrastable environments within maintenance-free dry cryostats are needed for high-precision surface probe microscopy experiments, as well as next-generation quantum technologies. The most demanding applications require picometre-scale precision combined with multi-axis and millimetre-scale scanning range, while offering access to optical, microwave, and radiofrequency control and a vector magnetic field. We demonstrate a versatile platform for such systems based on passive and active vibration control for a commercial dry cryostat. Using a tunable optical microcavity as a sensor, we report vibration levels of 4.2 pm root mean square at 2.3 K over one hour without postselection. We further demonstrate drift-free long-term operation with stability below 8.6 pm RMS over 12 hours. Our system enables continuous and automated operation for next-generation high-throughput applications without the need for liquid helium infrastructure. Requiring only standard machining facilities and commercially available hardware, the design can be readily adapted for cryogenic optical, electrical and magnetic high-precision measurements across quantum science, surface science, and nanotechnology.

title: Vibro-polaritonic Raman spectroscopy via cavity Born-Oppenheimer perturbation theory
abstract: We derive a vibro-polaritonic Raman activity from third-order cavity Born-Oppenheimer perturbation theory (CBO-PT) accounting for weak interactions between electrons and low-frequency cavity modes in the vibrational strong coupling (VSC) regime. This work extends the recently presented CBO-PT linear response approach [J. Phys. Chem. Lett. 2024, 15, 2262-2269] from infrared (IR) to vibro-polaritonic Raman spectroscopy. In a first step, we discuss cavity-induced corrections to the static dipole polarizability tensor, which manifest as molecular and cavity mode contribution determined by the polarization-projected static hyperpolarizability tensor. We then obtain the corresponding vibro-polaritonic Raman activity in double harmonic approximation, which contains molecular, cavity and mixed contributions similar to previously discussed CBO-PT IR intensities. The cavity Raman activity can be interpreted as effective transmission component, which is exclusively determined by the polaritonic Raman response. The methodology and its relation to vibro-polaritonic IR spectroscopy is illustrated for a formaldehyde molecule under VSC. An implementation of the CBO-PT linear response approach for vibro-polaritonic Raman and IR spectroscopies is provided via the open-source Python package CBOvibSpec.

title: A compact, dual-colour chirped-pulse laser system for field-deployable coherent Rayleigh-Brillouin scattering diagnostics
abstract: Single-shot coherent Rayleigh-Brillouin scattering (CRBS) requires dual colour, frequency, and pulse duration agile laser systems, currently available only in laboratory layouts. In this work, we present a compact, portable, and robust next generation laser system that meets all of these requirements. Key features include an integrated master-slave seed laser design for stable frequency chirping, fiber-coupled acousto-optic modulator (AOM) gated pulse shaping for long-term thermal stability, and customized amplification stages in a rugged, portable enclosure which simplifiy the alignment and maintenance process. The system in this implementation can deliver up to $450$~mJ per arm, chirp rates up to $\sim22$~MHz$/$ns, and arbitrary temporal profiles within $\sim25$~ns to $\sim1$~$\mu$s. This laser system is validated by measuring the neutral number density of an atmospheric plasma jet, and a two-dimensional temperature map is constructed, demonstrating lab-grade diagnostics for field deployment.

title: Noise suppression of quantum frequency conversion in thin-film lithium niobate waveguides via adapted poling
abstract: Quantum frequency conversion (QFC) enables optical interfaces between dissimilar quantum systems, but suppressing noise while maintaining high conversion efficiency remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate that adapted poling in thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) waveguides reduces the pump-power requirement while shifting the dominant noise mechanism and its power scaling. In 2-cm-long waveguides, adapted poling enables maximum conversion efficiency at an on-chip pump power of $19\pm0.8$~mW, reducing the required pump power by 8~dB and the total conversion noise by 14~dB relative to conventional periodic poling at their respective maximum-conversion operating points. Controlled measurements with different pump conditions and device configurations reveal a transition from predominantly quadratic noise scaling in periodically poled devices to predominantly linear scaling in adapted-poling devices. This transition accompanies a shift from noise dominated by cascaded second-harmonic generation and Stokes spontaneous Raman scattering to direct anti-Stokes spontaneous Raman scattering. These results establish adapted poling as an effective approach to suppressing nonlinear noise, enabling low-noise integrated frequency converters for quantum networks.

title: Magnetic flux ring splitting near a Navier-Stokes singularity
abstract: OpenAI reports a forced Navier-Stokes flow that becomes singular in finite time, raising the question of its physical consequences. Magnetic reconnection offers a test through the splitting and merging of flux structures. We use resistive magnetohydrodynamics to simulate a magnetic ring driven by an imposed, regularized flow that reproduces the geometry and scaling of the collapsing core. At the nominal singular time, we remove the imposed drive and allow the system to evolve freely. Reconnections before and after release split the ring into two or more daughter rings through bifurcations of the poloidal flux function, with Lorentz feedback selecting the bifurcation type. Unequal winding by the swirl above and below the midplane produces asymmetric toroidal magnetic stresses, unfolding the kinematic pitchfork-like transition into a fold. For single-island splits, the cusp normal form predicts the asymmetry of the daughter rings without adjustable parameters. Three-dimensional simulations retain the splits and merger, confirming that approach to hydrodynamic blow-up can trigger magnetic restructuring.

title: Resonant pair production and flat band melting in a driven Rydberg chain
abstract: We study a Rydberg chain subjected to a two-tone periodic drive of the detuning $\Delta(t)$ and Rabi frequency $\Omega(t)$ at frequencies $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2=\nu \omega_1$ respectively with $\nu \in \mathbf{Z}$. In the strong Rydberg blockade limit, such a system reduces to the PXP model and exhibits exact Floquet flat band. Here we determine, using a time-dependent Schrieffer-Wolff transformation, the domain of validity of such PXP dynamics once the blockade-violating processes are taken into account. We study the melting of such flat bands in the presence of strong, but finite, blockade strength. Using Floquet perturbation theory (FPT), we identify two mechanisms for such melting; the first occurs due to the presence of many-body resonances involving resonant production of nearest-neighbor Rydberg excitation pairs while the second involves virtual processes that access intermediate states with such pairs. Our analytical FPT results match with those obtained using exact diagonalization on a finite chain. We study the dynamics for $|{\rm vac}\rangle$ (Fock state with no Rydberg excitation), $|{\mathbb {Z}}_2\rangle$, and $|{\mathbb {Z}}_3\rangle$ (Fock states with Rydberg excitations on alternate and every third site respectively) initial states. We find that $|{\rm vac}\rangle$ shows exceptional stability against resonant pair formation while $|{\mathbb {Z}}_3\rangle$ exhibits flat band melting via virtual processes away from the direct resonances. We find oscillatory dynamics with large time period for the $|{\mathbb {Z}}_2\rangle$ initial state and the presence of Floquet scars that have large overlap with $|{\mathbb {Z}}_3\rangle$ state; these phenomena occur due to processes that are absent in the PXP limit. We propose measurement of nearest neighbor pair correlation functions using Rydberg atom quantum simulator platforms as an accessible experimental probe for these effects.

title: Chirality-resolved imaging of spin waves with a quantum spin
abstract: Spin waves carry their propagation direction in the handedness of their circularly polarized stray field, a property inaccessible to scalar magnetometers. In the Damon-Eshbach surface wave of an in-plane magnetized film, the dipolar field above the film rotates with a handedness fixed by the direction of travel. The nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centre in diamond is an intrinsic polarization analyser: a right-handed field about the NV axis drives one spin transition, and a left-handed field drives the other, in both the ground and the excited state. Here, we exploit the two excited-state transitions, which lie inside the spin-wave band of yttrium iron garnet (YIG), as a pair of chirality channels and image Damon-Eshbach waves in both directions. Because reflection from an etched boundary reverses the handedness, the incident and reflected waves appear as two lines in one spectrum and are imaged separately. In the ground state, the same rule applies, and the selected field drives Rabi oscillations, a route to chirality-selective control of the NV spin by magnons. Reading the two channels gives the direction of a spin wave at one point, without a phase reference. This advances chirality-resolved quantum sensing and provides insight into chiral spin-wave dynamics.

title: Quantum Circuits for Variable-Coefficient Vlasov Dynamics via Schrödingerisation
abstract: High-dimensional Vlasov equations present promising use cases for quantum simulation, but their transport coefficients must be implemented coherently in order to preserve a compact quantum representation. We develop explicit Schrödingerised circuits for prescribed external field Vlasov dynamics without classical field updates. In 1D1V, velocity-dependent streaming is compiled directly from the encoded velocity register, while a non-linear cubic field is evaluated using reversible fixed-point arithmetic. For fixed polynomial degree, the field workspace scales linearly with the coordinate register width, while the field evaluation subroutine has polynomial depth. As a proof of concept, we simulate a minimal coupled 3D3V anharmonic Penning system and realise mixed electric-field terms and transverse magnetic coupling on a six-dimensional phase space in agreement with classical calculations. Resource analysis shows approximately linear growth with the number of time steps, while identifying the auxiliary register as the dominant depth bottleneck. Structured preparation and register recovery of the auxiliary state reveal an interplay between loading cost and readout. Together, our algorithm demonstrates a fully coherent quantum simulation of high-dimensional Vlasov dynamics with variable coefficients and identifies the practical resource costs that must be controlled for large-scale quantum implementation.

title: When Magnitude Suffices: Reconstructing Time-Domain-Gated Microwave Signals Without Phase on a Thoracic Phantom
abstract: Time-domain gating separates the arrivals that form a microwave S-parameter measurement. It requires the measurement of complex values, so this application almost always uses a vector network analyzer (VNA). We show that, on one calibrated measurement configuration, the gated magnitude the VNA would give can be reconstructed from a magnitude-only sweep of a spectrum analyzer with a tracking generator (SA). We select the gate center for separability of the measured states, correct each instrument once by a per-bin subtraction of a reference state, and train a fully connected network on sweeps from both instruments. The test object is a torso phantom with lung-shaped compartments whose filling takes eleven dielectric states, each held out in turn. On $S_{11}$ the reconstruction from SA input reaches a shape error of 0.08 dB$^2$ with a state ordering of 0.81. This matches the reconstruction from VNA input. On $S_{21}$ it reaches 0.82 dB$^2$ and keeps the ordered groups of the states. An explicit phase prediction performs much worse, because gating needs the phase to about 0.2 rad RMS. Across eleven measurement configurations the dependence of phase on magnitude is strong for reflection and weak for transmission. This explains the difference between $S_{11}$ and $S_{21}$. Where the magnitude carries enough of the phase, a scalar instrument gives the gated response without any phase measurement after installation. On the open UM-BMID breast data set, with whole phantoms held out, the shape error of the network is 30 percent lower than that of a per-bin linear map.

title: Gabor-Enhanced Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Fast Simulations of Acoustic Wavefields
abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have gained attention for solving partial differential equations, including the scattered Helmholtz equation, due to their flexibility and mesh-free formulation. However, their performance suffers from low-frequency bias, particularly in high-frequency wavefield simulations, limiting convergence speed and accuracy. To address this, we propose a novel and simplified PINN framework that incorporates explicit, trainable Gabor basis functions to efficiently capture the localized and oscillatory nature of wavefields. Unlike previous Gabor-based PINNs that rely on multiplicative filters or auxiliary networks to learn Gabor parameters, our approach redefines the network's task as learning a nonlinear mapping from input coordinates to a custom Gabor coordinate system, where a Gabor function captures the dominant oscillatory behavior of the wavefield. This formulation absorbs the effect of two Gabor parameters into the learned mapping, reducing computational complexity and eliminating the need for manual tuning of hyperparameters. We also present an efficient formulation for incorporating a Perfectly Matched Layer (PML) into the training by deriving real-valued loss components and introducing an analytical expression for the background wavefield. Numerical experiments on various velocity models show that our Gabor-PINN achieves faster convergence, higher accuracy, and greater robustness to architectural design and initialization compared to both traditional PINNs and prior Gabor-based methods. The improvement lies not in adding architectural complexity --as is common in enhanced PINNs -- but in absorbing this complexity into the learned coordinate transformation, making the method both simpler and more effective. Our implementation is publicly available to support reproducibility and future research.

title: Towards Low-Energy Electron High-Resolution Spectroscopy with Transition-Edge Sensors
abstract: We present a study of the energy resolution of transition-edge sensors (TESs) for the detection of electrons in the 100~eV kinetic energy range. The TES is a Ti-Au bilayer with an active area of ($60 \times 60$) $\mu$m$^2$ and a critical temperature of $\sim 80$~mK. The electron source is based on vertically-aligned multiwall carbon nanotubes located inside the cryostat, with electrons generated via field emission. For electrons in the $(92 - 99)$~eV kinetic energy range, we obtain a Gaussian energy resolution for fully-absorbed electrons of ($0.48 \pm 0.04 \pm 0.06$)~eV, where the first uncertainty is statistical and the second systematic}. When considering the full-width at half-maximum of the peak \textcolor{black}{of the signal amplitude distribution}, the corresponding resolution is of ($1.4 \pm 0.2 \pm 0.3$)~eV. The former represents an improvement of $(47-60)\%$ with respect to previous results, and is mainly attributed to the reduction in the TES active area. The latter is instead an improvement of over a factor of 21, and is mainly due to the reduction in the emitting area of the electron source, which significantly suppresses electron back-scattering in proximity of the TES. These results represent a major milestone towards high-precision spectroscopy on low-energy electrons, which is a key objective for the PTOLEMY experiment.

title: Machine Learning on Heterogeneous, Edge, and Quantum Hardware for Particle Physics (ML-HEQUPP)
abstract: The next generation of particle physics experiments will face a new era of challenges in data acquisition, due to unprecedented data rates and volumes along with extreme environments and operational constraints. Harnessing this data for scientific discovery demands real-time inference and decision-making, intelligent data reduction, and efficient processing architectures beyond current capabilities. Crucial to the success of this experimental paradigm are several emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML), silicon microelectronics, and the advent of quantum algorithms and processing. Their intersection includes areas of research such as low-power and low-latency devices for edge computing, heterogeneous accelerator systems, reconfigurable hardware, novel codesign and synthesis strategies, readout for cryogenic or high-radiation environments, and analog computing. This white paper presents a community-driven vision to identify and prioritize research and development opportunities in hardware-based ML systems and corresponding physics applications, contributing towards a successful transition to the new data frontier of fundamental science.

title: Nested active pointing control for interspacecraft laser interferometry
abstract: Precise pointing control is critical for interspacecraft laser interferometry, as angular misalignment introduces measurement noise and can even lead to laser link loss. We present a nested control architecture that uses differential wavefront sensing signals to drive a fast steering mirror (FSM) to track the incoming beam, while feeding the FSM deflections back to the attitude and orbit control system to suppress angle-dependent optical path variations. This scheme is experimentally validated in our hexapod-based setup. Relative to standalone FSM actuation, the nested configuration reduced the low-frequency root-mean-square pointing jitter by approximately a factor of 2 over 3--70 mHz in both directions. Additionally, tilt-to-length coupling was suppressed by an order of magnitude below 5 mHz and by two orders of magnitude below 0.5 mHz. These results demonstrate the feasibility of nested active pointing control for future interspacecraft laser interferometry missions.

title: Beyond white- and black-box modeling tools in optical communications and optical computing: physics-informed data-driven modeling
abstract: Efficient optimization and control of photonic computing and communication systems increasingly rely on accurate surrogate models/digital twins. While data-driven models may achieve faster inference than traditional physics-based methods, they typically suffer from poor training data efficiency and limited generalizability. To address this trade-off, physics-informed data-driven modeling has emerged as a powerful hybrid paradigm. This paper presents a comparative analysis of these three modeling paradigms across three test use cases: optical amplifiers, directly modulated lasers, and interferometer meshes. By evaluating model complexity, data efficiency, generalizability, and modularity, this work provides a detailed analysis of the respective trade-offs and highlights the advantages of combining physical insight with data-driven learning.

title: Optical Characterization Measurements of Commercial Polyvinyltoluene Scintillators for Accurate Geant4 Detector Modeling
abstract: Accurate Monte Carlo simulation of plastic scintillator detectors requires precise wavelength-dependent optical properties. We present measurements of wavelength-dependent refractive index $n(\lambda)$ and bulk absorption length $L_{\mathrm{abs}}(\lambda)$ for six commercial polyvinyltoluene (PVT)-based scintillators (Saint Gobain BC-400, BC-404, BC-408, BC-418, BC-422, and BC-430) at five wavelengths between 372 and 660 nm. Using a precision refraction apparatus and variable-thickness transmission measurements, we characterize material-specific dispersion that deviates substantially from both the manufacturer specification and literature values for pure PVT. Illustrative Geant4 simulations of a BC-422 detector demonstrate a 7.2% reduction in photocathode energy-deposition threshold events when using our measured $n(\lambda)$ compared to the constant manufacturer value, highlighting the practical importance of accurate optical property data for detector design and calibration. We successfully measure absorption lengths for BC-430 at four wavelengths between 372 and 505 nm (2.2-12.4 mm) and for all materials at 372 nm (2.2-38 mm), while establishing lower bounds exceeding 750 mm for weakly absorbing formulations at longer wavelengths.

title: Compact Fully Integrated Alignment-Free and Linearly Polarized Ho$^{3+}$ Single-Frequency Waveguide Laser
abstract: We report, for the first time, a fully integrated Ho$^{3+}$-doped fluoride glass waveguide laser incorporating a femtosecond laser-inscribed waveguide and waveguide Bragg grating. A line-by-line inscription technique was employed to fabricate the Bragg gratings, yielding highly consistent and reproducible grating characteristics with precise control of the Bragg resonance wavelength. A compact 12.4 mm cavity achieves stable single-frequency lasing at 2062.21 nm with a linewidth of less than 5 MHz. The laser exhibits intrinsically linearly polarized emission. This alignment-free architecture provides a compact and robust platform for integrated mid-infrared single-frequency laser sources.

title: Programmable Hard-X-Ray Spectral Comb Generation via Laser-Compton Scattering
abstract: Independent control of line spacing and offset underpins programmable frequency-comb spectroscopy, yet it has not been established for hard-X-ray sources based on inverse Compton scattering after electron transport and angular collection. Self-consistent multi-particle tracking and Li'enard-Wiechert radiation calculations model a transported 10 pC beam and its angle-integrated spectrum near 11 keV. Laser pulse separation programs the comb spacing, while pulse-to-pulse phase translates the entire line grid at fixed spacing. The spacing model agrees within 0.52%, while transport and optics change the phase-transfer slope by less than 0.2%. At fixed electron spot size, the largest resolvable separation scales as the inverse square of normalized emittance; subnanometer bunches also produce a mode-locked train with 13.9 as spacing. This two-coordinate programmability enables phase-stepped multicolor measurements and offers routes to hard-X-ray Ramsey interferometry, coherent control of core and nuclear excitations, and attosecond nonlinear spectroscopy.

title: A Rydberg atom array coupled to a high-cooperativity optical cavity
abstract: Integrating Rydberg-state control of atom-atom interactions with cavity control of atom-light interactions enables the combination of local entangling operations with photon-mediated long-range coupling, measurement, and communication. Such integration is challenging because electric fields generated by charges on cavity optics and by cavity-stabilizing actuators may disturb Rydberg-state coherence. Here, we couple a Rydberg tweezer array to a high-cooperativity optical cavity, suppressing the electric fields produced by cavity length actuation so that the residual field variation of about $3~\mathrm{mV/cm}$ rms does not limit Rydberg coherence. We demonstrate two capabilities that neither system provides alone. First, we use Purcell-enhanced fluorescence to read out atoms directly in the ground-Rydberg basis within $7.5~\mu\mathrm{s}$, well within the Rydberg-state lifetime, with ground- and Rydberg-state detection infidelities of $3\%$ and $5\%$, respectively, and with low atom loss. Second, we use Rydberg-Rydberg interactions to control collective light-atom scattering into the cavity mode. Specifically, we drive blockaded Rabi oscillations between a state with two ground-state atoms, which scatter collectively with a superradiant or subradiant rate controlled by the atomic positions, and an entangled state with a single Rydberg excitation, which scatters like a single atom. These capabilities open routes toward networked Rydberg processors, mid-circuit measurements in analog quantum simulators, and many-body quantum optics with entangled emitters coupled collectively to light.

title: Frequency comb stability, bistability, and self-starting in normal dispersion microresonators
abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that it is possible to generate frequency combs in normal dispersion microresonators by taking advantage of fabricated mode coupling that induces a mode split. In particular, photonic crystal resonators periodically modulate the microresonator's width, which geometrically creates mode coupling. In contrast to frequency combs generated by microresonators in the anomalous dispersion regime, which are typically generated using bright solitons, the frequency combs generated by normal dispersion regime microresonators are dark pulses that are commonly referred to as dark solitons or platicons. In this work, we examine the linear stability of platicons in the pump-detuning and pump-power parameter space as the mode split strength and cavity dispersion is varied. Our work reveals a broad region of stability for platicons. Our work also reveals the existence of fingers at high power at whose boundaries a sharp transition occurs and inside of which platicon solutions are bistable. Finally, we investigate the overlap of the region where platicons are stable with the region where continuous waves are modulationally unstable, and it is possible for a platicon to self-start. Simulations show that platicons consistently self-start inside this region.

title: Differentiable design of the PIAA-ZWFS: a flexible wavefront sensor that approaches the fundamental limit
abstract: Extreme adaptive optics (AO) is necessary for high contrast astronomy at scales of the habitable zone of nearby systems. We seek to evaluate wavefront sensors that approach fundamental limits of wavefront sensing, enabling adaptive optics systems to run faster or on fainter targets. We present the phase-induced amplitude apodisation Zernike wavefront sensor (PIAA-ZWFS): an adaptation of the conventional Zernike wavefront sensor (ZWFS) that leverages lossless apodisation of the pupil to concentrate the starlight in the focal plane. We optimise and evaluate the sensor with a differentiable modelling framework, drawing on concepts from Bayesian experimental design to minimise the variance of a maximum likelihood estimator that uses the system in the high Strehl regime. Our architecture shows state-of-the-art performance in simulation for different apertures, bandwidths, photon fluxes and source sizes, closing the gap to the fundamental limit by a factor 10 (2.5) compared to the conventional ZWFS (optimised ZWFS) in a typical photon-limited case. For extended sources, we show that even an ideal point source sensor rapidly becomes sub-optimal, and our system outperforms it for stellar diameters larger than 0.8{\lambda}/D. We verify that these gains do not come at the cost of dynamic range with either linear or non-linear reconstructors. Finally, we present a proof that there must be a trade-off between the information gained about amplitude and phase errors for any wavefront sensor. The PIAA-ZWFS is a viable wavefront sensor operating near the fundamental sensitivity limits.

title: Geometric inflation of deviations challenges neural quantum states in dynamics of quantum Ising models
abstract: Neural quantum states (NQS) have emerged as a powerful framework for simulating non-equilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated quantum systems, offering scalable variational representations of highly entangled states. Yet, accurate NQS simulations have been found to be surprisingly challenging in some physical regimes of limited complexity. Here, we address paradigmatic quench dynamics of a one-dimensional quantum Ising model as a controlled benchmark. Through supervised state reconstruction we establish substantially tighter empirical upper bounds on the required parameter count than previous estimates, ruling out representational limitations as the key obstruction. Instead, we uncover a geometric inflation of small deviations as a hitherto overlooked challenge for accurate solutions of the infinitesimal time-dependent variational principle (TDVP): the dynamical rotation of the kernel of the quantum geometric tensor (QGT) can suddenly lend physical significance to previously irrelevant parameter deviations. The stability of matrix product state solutions of the same TDVP suggests that the non-linearity of the neural network ansatz is the origin of the sensitivity. These results identify QGT-null-space rotation as a geometric diagnostic of sensitive NQS dynamics and as a concrete target for improving TDVP algorithms.

title: Path-Degenerate Quantum Interferometry for Loss Resilience in Gravitational-Wave Detectors
abstract: Optical decoherence degrades quantum correlations in squeezed states of light, severely limiting the quantum-nondemolition (QND) sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors. Here, we propose the path-degenerate quantum interferometry scheme that obviates the need for entire optical subsystems---including additional filter cavities, auxiliary parametric amplifiers, and Faraday isolators---thereby drastically reducing spatial mode mismatches while inherently integrating variational output, a long-standing theoretical proposal to further deepen the QND regime. We experimentally demonstrate a core aspect of this scheme, achieving a shot-noise-preserving signal enhancement that directly counteracts the detrimental effects of readout loss. By delivering an improved signal-to-quantum-noise ratio solely through the consolidation and reduction of currently considered optical subsystems, our approach offers a highly optimized route toward enhanced quantum-noise reduction in upcoming LIGO upgrades and next-generation gravitational-wave observatories.

title: Residual diagnostics for detecting the breakdown of the single power-law approximation in photoelectron yield spectroscopy: application to doped silicon
abstract: Our automated analysis of photoelectron yield spectroscopy (PYS) estimates the threshold Ith and the exponent n of a single power law for every spectrum. When this model fits poorly, however, the analysis cannot tell whether the data or the model is at fault. Here we present residual diagnostics that separate the two causes. The exponent is scanned continuously on a 1/n-power fit with an Akaike information criterion (AIC) based on the mean absolute error (MAE), and the spread of the resulting Akaike weights ($P \times \Delta n$) quantifies the uncertainty of the estimate. The normalized MAE (NMAE) and the RMSE-to-MAE ratio (RMR) assess the data quality, the Durbin-Watson (DW) statistic assesses the model adequacy, and the three checks are reported in parallel. With criteria set from an Au reference, the diagnostics were applied to 60 continuous measurements in air of four HF-treated Si samples. For heavily doped p-type Si, DW fell below its criterion, whereas the means of NMAE and RMR remained within their criteria. Prompted by this flag, we fitted the spectrum with a two-component model with fixed exponents (n = 1 and 2.5); the AIC decreased by 56, DW increased from 0.86 to 1.99, and the two components set in at 4.70 and 5.28 eV. For heavily doped n-type Si, the change during air exposure was consistent with a single component. The diagnostics thus identify the spectra that require a multi-component analysis without assuming an emission mechanism.

title: Non-Monotonic Exciton Transport Efficiency in Multi-layer Ring-shaped Quantum Networks inspired by Photosystem I
abstract: Photosystem I (PSI) is one of the most efficient natural photosynthetic complexes and serves as a structural prototype for understanding excitation energy transfer (EET) and designing artificial light-harvesting systems. Here, we construct a multilayer elliptical-conical quantum network inspired by PSI to investigate how antenna architecture affects EET. Excitation dynamics are simulated using the quantum jump approach combined with coherent modified Redfield theory (QJA-CMRT). The transfer efficiency exhibits a pronounced nonmonotonic dependence on pigment density, reaching a maximum of 0.86 at x=6 in the five-layer network. The optimal configuration contains 91 pigments, close to the number of core antenna pigments in natural PSI. Our combined density-of-states and kinetic analyses reveal that this nonmonotonic dependence originates from a trade-off: at low pigment densities, enhanced band overlap promotes energy transfer, whereas at high densities, excessive exciton delocalization compromises funnel directionality and reduces efficiency; the optimal configuration is consequently achieved at x=6. These findings provide insights into PSI antenna organization and offer guidelines for designing efficient artificial light-harvesting systems.
